questions.question: Do I need a dedicated aggregating aspect to collect a custom class from every aspect in den, or can I gather it from all of `den.aspects` directly?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**No — you don't need a dedicated aggregating aspect. Den gathers a custom class directly; there is no "aggregator aspect" pattern for this.**

I read this in `denful/den` (branch `main`):

**1. Class *content* is collected from every included aspect, automatically.** When den resolves a class for a scope, the pipeline walks the aspect's `includes` graph (`nix/lib/aspects/fx/handlers/include.nix` → `emitIncludes`) and each aspect in that closure emits every class key it defines — built-in or custom — via `emitClassesHandler` (`nix/lib/aspects/fx/handlers/emit-classes.nix`, `emitClassKey` iterates the aspect's class keys). Each emission is appended by the class collector into `state.scopedClassImports[scope][class]`, deduped by `"<class>@<aspect-identity>"` (`nix/lib/aspects/fx/handlers/class-collector.nix`). The accumulated list is what feeds the target module system as its imports list. A custom class is just an attr key on the aspect; nothing about it is treated specially, so contributions from all included aspects merge on their own.

**2. Class *declarations* are also collected directly, not via an aspect.** `modules/aspect-schema.nix` scans `config.den.aspects` and every `den.ful.<ns>` namespace for `.classes.<name>` entries and folds them into `config.den.classes` (`collectFromAspects` over `config.den.aspects` ++ per-namespace collection → `config.den.classes = allClasses`). Its own comment: "Local namespace classes are collected by aspect-schema.nix." So declaring your custom class once is enough for the schema registry to see it.

**3. For routing the custom class into your configs**, the documented pattern (`docs/src/content/docs/guides/custom-classes.mdx`) is: register the class once (`den.classes.<name>`, optionally with `forwardTo`), then wire `den.batteries.forward` (with `fromAspect` pointing at the owning aspect) via a one-line include — e.g. the doc's example uses `den.schema.flake-parts.includes = [ den.policies.files-to-flake-parts ]` for a `files` class. That's a declaration at the schema tier, not an aspect that gathers anything.

**One caveat on "all of `den.aspects`":** the walk collects from the *reachable include closure* of the entity being resolved — its own `.aspect` plus `den.schema.<kind>.includes` plus per-instance `includes`, plus transitive `includes` (`nix/lib/resolve-entity.nix`, `includes = selfProvide ++ schemaIncludes ++ instanceCollection "includes"`). An aspect that no one includes is never walked, so its class content is never collected. If you want a given aspect's custom class applied to every host, the direct mechanism is the schema tier: `den.schema.host.includes = [ den.aspects.<that> ]` — one line, no aggregator.

questions.question: A den quirk whose values depend on `config` works with `pipe.transform` when consumed from another host, but on the same host the transformed value is wrong. Is that a bug?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**Yes — it was a real bug, and it's fixed.** What you're describing is den discussion [#713](https://github.com/denful/den/issues/713) ("pipe.transform for local config-dependent quirks", Oct 4 2026), fixed by [PR #723](https://github.com/denful/den/pull/723), merged into `main` on Oct 15 2026 as commit `631b034`. If you're seeing it today, your den is pinned to a rev older than `631b034` — check the `denful/den` node in your `flake.lock`/npins.

**Why the asymmetry happened** (mechanism, from `nix/lib/aspects/fx/assemble-pipes.nix` and the PR):

- A quirk value that depends on `config` (i.e. `{ config, ... }: …`) emitted by the *consuming scope itself* cannot exist until that scope's `evalModules` fixpoint runs. Until then it is only a `__configThunk` marker (resolved later in `class-module.nix`'s `resolveMarkers`).
- Pipe value stages run *before* that, in `assemble-pipes.nix`, so pre-fix they met the unresolved marker: `filter`/`transform` passed it through **unchanged and silently skipped the stage** (your report), while `fold`/`for` applied the stage fn to the marker itself ("attribute … missing"), and `pipe.expose` lifted the value untransformed.
- Cross-host values behave differently by construction: `collect`/`collectAll`/`broadcast` resolve config-dependent emits **eagerly against the source's instantiated config** (`hostConfigs`) *before* the stages run, so by the time `pipe.transform` ran, the peer's value was already concrete data — which is exactly why it "worked" from another host.

**The fix (one rule, not per-stage):** every value stage now goes through `deferredStage`. If any value in the list is still deferred, the whole stage is deferred: the values travel as one group marker `{ __configThunk = true; __group = values; __post = <stage>; }`, and `class-module` resolves the group members and then runs `__post` — so a config-dependent value sees exactly the stages a plain one does, in order. I verified this is in current source: `nix/lib/aspects/fx/assemble-pipes.nix` at `main` (HEAD `6e5e413`, Oct 15 2026) contains `deferredStage` with exactly that shape, and the reference docs (`docs/.../reference/quirks.mdx`, "Config-dependent thunks → Local scope") now state: "a stage that meets a deferred value is deferred with it and runs on the resolved list."

**Regression test:** `templates/ci/modules/deadbugs/issue-713-config-thunk-pipe-stages.nix` — 9 tests (transform, filter, fold, for, append+transform, withProvenance+transform, as+transform, to+transform, expose+transform on local config thunks). The PR reports 0/9 against pre-fix `main` and 9/9 with the fix; the full suite passed 1288/1288 at merge.

**One residual nuance (documented, not a bug):** even after the fix, the *resolution* semantics intentionally differ. A local thunk is resolved against the producer's **in-fixpoint** config (inside `evalModules`); a cross-host thunk is resolved against the source's **final instantiated** config. If your "wrong" value is one where the transform is now applied but the underlying `config` value you read differs between the two paths (e.g. an option that only settles after the fixpoint), that is the documented local-vs-cross-host difference, not the #713 defect.

questions.question: Does using den make Nix evaluation of my NixOS systems slower than wiring nixosSystem by hand?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Short answer: **no, not for the NixOS system evaluation itself — den ends up calling the exact same `nixpkgs.lib.nixosSystem` you'd call by hand, once per host, and only when that host's flake output is accessed.** What den adds is bookkeeping *around* that call, which is data-level work, not extra full NixOS evaluations — with one notable exception (below).

**How I know (checked in denful/den @ main):**

1. **Same function, once per host.** `nix/lib/entities/host.nix` defines the host's `instantiate` option: *"Function used to instantiate the OS configuration… `nixos`: inputs.nixpkgs.lib.nixosSystem"* with `default = inputs.nixpkgs.lib.nixosSystem`. Den doesn't wrap or re-implement the system builder; it picks the class's standard one (override `instantiate` if you need a custom input name or `specialArgs`).

2. **Lazy, like hand-written outputs.** In `nix/lib/aspects/fx/resolve.nix`, phase 4 (`applyInstantiates`) says: *"Lazy: spec.instantiate is NOT called eagerly. Each output leaf is a thunk that calls spec.instantiate only when accessed (e.g., when someone reads config.flake.nixosConfigurations.cortex). This avoids evaluating all hosts when only one is needed."* So `nixosConfigurations.foo` costs one `nixosSystem` call — identical to wiring it by hand.

3. **The extra work is data-level and memoized.** Before phase 4, den walks your aspect tree through a state-machine pipeline (`fx` handlers) to collect per-class modules, and runs its own small option registry (`den.hosts.*` submodules) plus one `lib.evalModules` for the "flake" entity (`modules/outputs.nix`). `nix/lib/entities/_types.nix` notes the resolve is declared as a module option *"so the module fixpoint memoizes it — every consumer … reads the same value, guaranteeing one resolve."* Module dedup across scopes is also done up front ("keeping duplicates wastes evaluation"). This is real extra evaluation work compared to a hand-rolled `nixosSystem`, but it's walks over your aspect definitions, not extra NixOS module-system runs.

**The one case where den does cost extra NixOS-scale evals:** the "B′" pass in `resolve.nix`. If any pipe/quirk value in your config is a *config-dependent* thunk (a function that needs a host's `.config` to resolve, i.e. cross-host "collect"-style pipes), den builds every peer host's **full `.config`** (`lib.mapAttrs (_: spec: (spec.instantiate (mkArgs spec)).config) specsByHost`) so those thunks can resolve. That's an additional full NixOS module-system evaluation per peer host — and it's gated: `hasAnyConfigThunk` is false for the common case, in which case *"hostConfigs stays null and assemblePipes skips cross-host instantiation entirely."*

**Practical take:** for a typical aspect-based config (no config-dependent cross-host pipes), expect roughly the same eval cost as hand-wired `nixosSystem` per accessed host plus a small constant overhead for den's resolve machinery. If you *do* use config-dependent pipes across hosts, expect a measurable extra cost and profile with `time nix flake check --no-build` / `nix eval` on the affected outputs.

Caveat: this is from reading den's source (`denful/den` @ main, files cited above) — I did not run a benchmark, so the magnitude of the overhead is not measured, and I couldn't check whether *your* config triggers the config-dependent-pipe pass.","confidence":0.72,"gaps":["No benchmark run: magnitude of den's extra evaluation overhead (and whether it is perceptible) is unmeasured","eval and clone were unavailable in this environment; source was read via web fetch of denful/den@main files, not a checked-out tree at a pinned rev","Not checked whether the asker's own config uses config-dependent cross-host pipes (the B′ pass that adds a full .config eval per peer host)"],"escalate_forced":"no"}

questions.question: Is a den policy essentially a transition function in a pipeline over my hosts and users?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Yes — that's essentially right, and den's source phrases it in almost those words.

**What the source says.** In `denful/den` at `main`:

- README (Principles): "Policy — how entities relate: topology and routing between them."
- `nix/lib/policy-effects.nix` header: "Policies return lists of these; the pipeline dispatches on `__policyEffect`." This file is `den.lib.policy` (see `nix/lib/default.nix`, `policy = ./policy-effects.nix`).
- `modules/policies/core.nix` header: "Core entity policies — fundamental traversal between entity kinds."

**The transition-function reading, concretely.** A policy is a function `ctx -> [effects]`, attached per node-kind via schema includes (e.g. `den.schema.host.includes = [ den.policies.host-to-users ]` in core.nix). The pipeline walks your entity graph (flake → systems → hosts/homes → users, plus any classes you invent), and at each node it dispatches that class's policies against the current context — the entity plus the accumulated aspect scope. So in your terms: state = (entity, its class, in-flight context); policies = the transitions out of that state.

The host→user policy is the clearest example: `den.policies.host-to-users = { host, ... }: ...` returns, per user the host declares, `[ resolve.shared { user } ]` (a fan-out that "creates a parallel branch — a sibling context with new bindings merged into parent") plus an `include` of any entity-named sub-aspect (e.g. `den.aspects.<host>.<user>`).

**Two refinements to the mental model:**

1. **The pipeline isn't only over hosts and users.** The built-in policies also cover the flake layer (`modules/policies/flake.nix`: `flake-to-systems`, `system-to-os-outputs`, `system-to-hm-outputs`, and per-output `packages/apps/checks/devShells/legacyPackages-to-flake` routes), and you can define your own classes — README: "Bring your own classes and whole pipelines… if you can walk it as data, Den can configure it." Host↔user is just the *core entity* policy layer.

2. **A transition doesn't just move you to the next entity.** What a policy returns is a list of effects, and only some are moves: `resolve`/`resolve.to` (context fan-out), `include`/`exclude` (add/remove an aspect in the current scope), `route`/`deliver` (a delivery edge `(S, T, P, M)` — move content collected from class S into class T at an attrpath, mode merge/nest/verbatim), `instantiate` (materialize that entity's final config, post-pipeline), `provide` (inject a new module that never came from the walk), `spawn` (deferred node), and `pipe` (named data pipes with stages: filter, transform, fold, append, for, broadcast, collect). "Transition function" captures the traversal part; the effect list is the payload each transition carries.

Policies also compose: `den.lib.policy.for <entity>` restricts one to specific entities (matched by `id_hash`), `when <pred>` gates it on a predicate, and `mkPolicy` names it.

**How I know:** read at `main` via raw fetches (clone was unavailable in this run) — `README.md`, `modules/policies/core.nix`, `modules/policies/flake.nix`, `nix/lib/policy-effects.nix`, `nix/lib/default.nix`. **What the source says.** In `denful/den` at `main`:

- README (Principles): "Policy — how entities relate: topology and routing between them."
- `nix/lib/policy-effects.nix` header: "Policies return lists of these; the pipeline dispatches on `__policyEffect`." This file is `den.lib.policy` (see `nix/lib/default.nix`, `policy = ./policy-effects.nix`).
- `modules/policies/core.nix` header: "Core entity policies — fundamental traversal between entity kinds."

**The transition-function reading, concretely.** A policy is a function `ctx -> [effects]`, attached per node-kind via schema includes (e.g. `den.schema.host.includes = [ den.policies.host-to-users ]` in core.nix). The pipeline walks your entity graph (flake → systems → hosts/homes → users, plus any classes you invent), and at each node it dispatches that class's policies against the current context — the entity plus the accumulated aspect scope. So in your terms: state = (entity, its class, in-flight context); policies = the transitions out of that state.

The host→user policy is the clearest example: `den.policies.host-to-users = { host, ... }: ...` returns, per user the host declares, `[ resolve.shared { user } ]` (a fan-out that "creates a parallel branch — a sibling context with new bindings merged into parent") plus an `include` of any entity-named sub-aspect (e.g. `den.aspects.<host>.<user>`).

**Two refinements to the mental model:**

1. **The pipeline isn't only over hosts and users.** The built-in policies also cover the flake layer (`modules/policies/flake.nix`: `flake-to-systems`, `system-to-os-outputs`, `system-to-hm-outputs`, and per-output `packages/apps/checks/devShells/legacyPackages-to-flake` routes), and you can define your own classes — README: "Bring your own classes and whole pipelines… if you can walk it as data, Den can configure it." Host↔user is just the *core entity* policy layer.

2. **A transition doesn't just move you to the next entity.** What a policy returns is a list of effects, and only some are moves: `resolve`/`resolve.to` (context fan-out), `include`/`exclude` (add/remove an aspect in the current scope), `route`/`deliver` (a delivery edge `(S, T, P, M)` — move content collected from class S into class T at an attrpath, mode merge/nest/verbatim), `instantiate` (materialize that entity's final config, post-pipeline), `provide` (inject a new module that never came from the walk), `spawn` (deferred node), and `pipe` (named data pipes with stages: filter, transform, fold, append, for, broadcast, collect). "Transition function" captures the traversal part; the effect list is the payload each transition carries.

Policies also compose: `den.lib.policy.for <entity>` restricts one to specific entities (matched by `id_hash`), `when <pred>` gates it on a predicate, and `mkPolicy` names it.

{"answer":"**Short answer:** den is a human-led project (written by its maintainer, vic / `denful`) with LLMs involved in the development process — and it has an explicit, written policy for AI-assisted contributions.

**How the code gets written**
- The docs themselves say it: *"LLMs have been involved in many aspects of building this project by most maintainers"* (`docs/src/content/docs/contributing.mdx`, "All Contributions Are Welcome").
- The repo ships agent tooling as a first-class part of the workflow: `AGENTS.md` (a long guide for AI coding agents covering repo layout, the fx pipeline, code style, and git conventions), `CLAUDE.md` (which is just `@AGENTS.md`), and `.agents/skills/den-debugging/SKILL.md` (a bug-fix workflow for agents, bridged into `.claude/skills/`). AI-assisted code contributions are accepted, provided contributors agree to:
1. Tag the issue/PR with the `ai-assisted` tag for tracking and accountability.

   - you recognize the AI-generated contribution as your own and are legally accountable for it;

questions.question: Is now a good time to start using den, or should I wait for the gen-based rewrite?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**Short answer: start now. There is no scheduled date to wait for, and starting today is not a dead end.**

Here's what I checked and what it means for you:

## The rewrite is "planned, not shipped"

Den's own docs page [`docs/src/content/docs/future.mdx` at `denful/den@main`](https://github.com/denful/den/blob/main/docs/src/content/docs/future.mdx) ("Future: den on gen") is explicit:

> **Planned, not shipped** — This section describes a design in progress. Names, APIs and timelines are not settled, and nothing here is available in den today.

The plan (aspects/hosts/users as nodes in one graph, policies as rules over that graph via gen-dispatch, one gen-scope evaluation layer) is a redesign of *how den decides which modules each host gets*. It is not a fork you're choosing between.

## Starting now doesn't strand you

The same page says the output stays ordinary NixOS, nix-darwin and home-manager modules, and that gen checks its merge behaviour against nixpkgs' module system **byte for byte on every change**:

> The modules you write today are the modules a gen-based den builds.

And den is already *on* gen in part: the typed registries behind `den.hosts`, `den.homes` and every `den.schema.<kind>` are gen-schema instance types (content-addressed `id_hash` included). den declares no flake inputs of its own and loads gen through the gen hub. So the rewrite extends what den does, rather than replacing what you write.

## The real risk is v0.x churn, and it's manageable

Den is at v0.x. Per its [versioning page](https://den.denful.dev/releases/): "That does not mean it is unstable, we have >180 tests in our CI… what v0.x means is that Den development is currently fast-paced, evolving and being shaped by its current users." In practice the last months show real API movement — e.g. the Oct 12 commit *#717 "migrate to gen-schema's options-first API"* deprecates the old kind-first `den.lib.schema.mkInstanceType` call (it now prints a deprecation warning telling you to swap the arguments).

Mitigations, all stated by the project:

- **Pin to the `latest` tag** (`github:denful/den/latest`) instead of tracking `main` if you only want release points; read release notes, since they carry the important changes.
- **Watch the `heads-up` announcements** (tagged commits, also forwarded to the Zulip and Matrix channels) when you do track main.
- The latest commit (Oct 15, 2026) reports the full CI suite passing at **1318/1318**, and den is running on real fleets, including internal infra at The European Commission.

## Recommendation

- **New config:** start now with today's den — `inputs.den.url = "github:denful/den/latest"` (or pin a specific release), and follow the "From Zero to Den" guide. You get the framework today; you inherit the rewrite later without rewriting your modules.
- **Migrating from flake/dendritic:** same advice, via the "Migrate to Den" guide.
- **If you specifically want gen's pure-stack benefits** (the 1.6×–2.8× eval speedup, graph queries, incremental re-evaluation): those are the planned, not shipped, part — nothing is dated you can wait for, and today's den already carries the gen-schema identity layer.

**How I know:** `denful/den@main` README (fetched raw), `docs/src/content/docs/future.mdx` and the releases/versioning page, the den commit history (latest: `6e5e413`, Oct 15 2026), and the `sini/gen` hub README, which lists the 23-library roster and its `rehost-den-parity` byte-parity oracle over den's registry shape.","confidence":0.8,"gaps":["eval and clone were unavailable in this environment, so I did not evaluate denful/den at rev 6e5e413 myself (the repo's own CI reports 1318/1318 tests passing on that commit)","the 1.6x-2.8x speedup numbers are as stated in den's docs citing gen's 2026-07-04 audit; I did not run the benchmarks","no explicit release-date target for the gen-based rewrite exists in the docs; 'timelines are not settled' is the project's own statement, not a dated milestone"],"escalate_forced":"no"}

questions.question: How are the ordinary nixpkgs NixOS modules used by den and by gen? Are they wrapped or rewritten?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Neither framework rewrites ordinary nixpkgs NixOS modules — both use them unmodified. The only "wrap" is a thin boundary layer at the crossing into nixpkgs; the only thing actually *rewritten* is gen's **own** module system (a pure re-implementation of `lib.evalModules` for gen's own module trees, not for nixpkgs modules).

**den** (`sini/den`, fork of denful/den)
- Den itself is just ordinary NixOS modules layered onto the user's tree: `nix/flakeModule.nix` imports `modules/` into the consumer's NixOS module tree, and `modules/options.nix` declares a `den.*` options subtree (`den.hosts`, `den.aspects`, `den.classes`, `den.quirks`, `den.schema`), with built-in classes `nixos` and `darwin`. Nothing in nixpkgs is modified or vendored.
- Aspect class content stays a plain module: `nix/lib/aspects/types.nix` states "NixOS module functions (taking lib/config/options) are **NOT** coerced". The `aspectContentType` wrapper only adds provenance metadata (`__contentValues`, `__provider`) — a wrapper of record, not a rewrite of the module body.
- Final evaluation is the consumer's own nixpkgs: README — "Den embraces your Nix … **Zero dependencies.** Every part is optional and replaceable." So the `nixos` class module goes to whatever nixpkgs eval the user already has; nixpkgs modules run as-is.

**gen** (hub `sini/gen` + the gen-* libraries)
- The rewrite is gen's own module system, not nixpkgs' modules: gen-merge "reproduces `lib.evalModules` + `lib.types` merge output with **zero nixpkgs**", all 23 roster libraries are nixpkgs-lib-free (enforced by a source scanner), and "full nixpkgs enters at the terminals alone."
- The user's ordinary nixpkgs NixOS modules pass through untouched: in the hub's `flakeModules/default.nix`, `gen.extraModules` is `attrsOf (listOf types.deferredModule)` — the comment: "**these are nixpkgs NixOS modules handed to `nixpkgs.lib.nixosSystem`**" — delivered to `realize` as `extraModules.nixos.<node>`.
- The only nixpkgs contact is a thin terminal adapter: the default `nixos` terminal is `genBind.crossing.mkHostedTerminal { evaluator = cfg.nixpkgs.lib.nixosSystem; … }` (consumer-overridable / suppressible). In `sini/gen-bind` `lib/crossing-adapter-set.nix`, `wrapUnit` is `evaluator { modules = body ++ extraModules; specialArgs = { nodes = admittedExtent; } // passthrough; }` — the plain module list is appended and handed straight to nixpkgs' own `lib.nixosSystem`.

- The boundary is what `sini/hola` tests: a "parity harness for a pure-gen module engine that hosts **unmodified nixpkgs modules**."

questions.question: If I give a NixOS option the wrong shape inside a den aspect, does den catch it when it resolves the aspect?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**No** — den does not catch a wrongly-shaped NixOS option when it resolves the aspect. The type error comes later, from the NixOS module system, when the resolved system is instantiated (i.e. when the flake output attribute is forced).

**How it works (denful/den @ main):**

1. **Aspect resolution is a pure data pipeline.** The fx pipeline (`nix/lib/aspects/fx/`) walks the `includes` DAG, collects per-class entries, and wraps each class module *function* with the den context args (partial application + collision policy, `class-module.nix` → `wrapFunctionModule`). The resolve result is a list of module functions/attrsets — data. Nothing in the pipeline feeds your `nixos` content through `evalModules`, so option values are never type-checked during resolution.

2. **The NixOS module system runs at instantiation, and lazily.** Phase 4 (`applyInstantiates`, `nix/lib/aspects/fx/resolve.nix`) builds the flake output tree as thunks: *"spec.instantiate is NOT called eagerly. Each output leaf is a thunk that calls spec.instantiate only when accessed."* `spec.instantiate` is `host.instantiate`, which defaults to `inputs.nixpkgs.lib.nixosSystem` (`nix/lib/entities/host.nix`). So `nixosSystem`'s `evalModules` — the thing that raises *"The option `…` is of type `…` but has value of type `…`"* — only runs when you first force e.g. `nixosConfigurations.<name>.config` (`nix flake check`, `nix eval .#…`, `nix build`).

**What den *does* catch at resolution time** (den-level shapes, not NixOS option values):
- Strict schema kinds (`den.schema.<kind> = den.lib.strict` / `isStrict`): closes the entity/aspect declaration freeform, so undeclared keys in your *den-level* declarations (host/user/aspect/home) are refused when den's flake module is evaluated (`nix/lib/strict.nix`, `modules/options.nix`).
- A class module function requesting a den context arg unavailable in that scope → warning *"den: class module requests 'X' but no X context is available"* and the entry is dropped as unsatisfied (`class-module.nix`).
- A den context arg colliding with a module-system arg → throw under the default `collisionPolicy = "error"` (`den.config.classModuleCollisionPolicy`, `modules/config.nix`): *"den: class module arg 'X' collides with module-system arg — set collisionPolicy to resolve"*.
- Bad `includes`/`excludes` elements at the schema tier → throw in the option `apply` (`checkCollectionElement`, `modules/options.nix`).

**Practical gotcha:** den rewrites wrapped modules' file location to a synthetic `class@<aspect-identity>` (`wrapModule`, `nix/lib/aspects/fx/wrap-classes.nix`), so when NixOS's type error finally fires, the location it cites points at that wrapper string rather than at your aspect file.

How I know: read den's source at `denful/den` @ `main` (current rev; `clone` was unavailable in this eval, so I read files over the web) — `nix/lib/aspects/fx/resolve.nix` (lazy `applyInstantiates`), `nix/lib/entities/host.nix` (`instantiate` default), `nix/lib/aspects/fx/class-module.nix` and `wrap-classes.nix` (arg wrapping, collision, location rewrite), `nix/lib/strict.nix` + `modules/options.nix` (strict schema, collection checks).","confidence":0.85,"gaps":["Did not run a live eval reproducing a NixOS type error from a den aspect (no committed wrong-shape aspect in the repo); the answer is derived from source reads at denful/den@main","Verified the built-in nixos/darwin root-class path; did not check third-party batteries (e.g. home-manager) for eager evaluation of class content that might surface type errors earlier"],"escalate_forced":"no"}

questions.question: The den docs show named sub-aspects as `den.aspects.igloo.<name>`. Is that the same thing as `den.aspects.igloo.provides.<name>`?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Yes — they refer to the same aspect. `provides` (with `_` as its alias) is the *legacy* spelling for sub-aspects, and the direct `den.aspects.igloo.<name>` key is the current form. Den makes them identical by forwarding `provides` children onto the aspect's top level when the aspect is merged.

**How I know:**

1. **The docs you're quoting say exactly this.** `den`'s own docs (`docs/src/content/docs/explanation/aspects.mdx`, "Nested aspects"): *"Older configurations nest under `provides` (alias `_`), as in `den.aspects.<aspect>.provides.<name>`. 2. **The source does the forwarding.** In `denful/den` at main (`6e5e413`), `nix/lib/aspects/types.nix`:
   - `aspectSubmodule` wires `_` as a module-system alias of `provides`: `(lib.mkAliasOptionModule [ "_" ] [ "provides" ])`.
   - `mergeWithAspectMeta` returns `providesChildren // merged // { … }`, with the comment: *"Forward provides children onto the merged aspect so that `aspect.docker` resolves to `aspect.provides.docker`. provides-first so direct freeform keys on merged take priority."* The nested version (`aspectContentType.merge`) does the same: *"Forward provides children onto the wrapper so that `aspect.child.monitoring` resolves to `aspect.child.provides.monitoring`."*

questions.question: An aspect does `{ host, ... }: lib.optionalAttrs (host ? gpu) { ... }`. Who sets `host.gpu`, and where?

function.name: reply

draft.answer:
**You set it — it's not den's.** `host.gpu` is a *freeform attribute on the host entity*, and host entities are user data. The `host` argument an aspect receives is the fully resolved host entity from your own flake, so `gpu` only exists there if someone (you, your team, a shared aspect's schema) put it on the host declaration.

**Where it lives:** in your config repo, in the file that declares `den.hosts` (in den's own template that's `templates/default/modules/hosts.nix`; in your repo, wherever your hosts file is):

```nix
den.hosts.x86_64-linux.igloo = {
  gpu = "nvidia";      # freeform — no option declaration needed
  datacenter = "eu-west";
};
```

If you want the attribute on *every* host with a default, declare it once in the kind's schema instead:

```nix
den.schema.host = { options.gpu = lib.mkOption { default = null; type = lib.types.str; }; };
```

That's exactly the pattern from den's docs (`docs/src/content/docs/explanation/entities.mdx`, "Freeform attributes"): hosts, users and homes use `freeformType`, so arbitrary data you attach to an entity is reachable in aspects through the entity's context argument — `{ host, ... }: lib.optionalAttrs (host ? gpu) { ... }`.

**How the value gets to the aspect (verified in `sini/den` @ `main`):**
- `nix/lib/entities/host.nix` — `den.hosts` is `attrsOf (submodule { freeformType = deepMergeAttrs })` and the host instance type is `mkInstanceType den.schema.host { strict = false; … }`, so any attribute on a host instance (like `gpu`) is kept, not rejected.
- `nix/lib/entities/_types.nix` — `resolvedCtxModule` builds `config.resolved = den.lib.resolveEntity kind (ctx // { ${kind} = config })`, i.e. the *whole* host config becomes the `host` context value.
- `nix/lib/resolve-entity.nix` — `entity = ctx.${name}` and `scopeHandlers = constantHandler augmentedCtx`, so the aspect's `host` is that resolved entity, freeform attributes included. Nothing in den populates `gpu`; it just threads your declaration through.

**One gotcha:** if your flake imports `inputs.den.flakeModules.strict`, freeform is off — `gpu` must then be a declared option (via `den.schema.host`), otherwise the host declaration throws a `STRICT MODE` error naming the missing option.

So: grep your own repo for `den.hosts` / `den.schema.host` — `gpu = …` has to be there for `host ? gpu` to be true. If it isn't set anywhere, the `optionalAttrs` block simply never fires (and that's the intended use: the shape of the data is the condition).

questions.question: How deep can den aspects nest, and does including `den.aspects.foo._` include grandchildren and foo's own class keys too?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**Nesting depth: no hard limit.** Aspect nesting is recursive by construction: `provides` is declared as `lib.types.submodule { freeformType = lib.types.lazyAttrsOf (providerType …) }`, and every freeform key is wrapped by `aspectContentType`, which gives the nested attrset its own `provides` and its own `_`. So `den.aspects.foo.bar.baz.…` works to any depth — the CI suite tests 3 levels (`den.aspects.top.mid.deep`, `den.aspects.infra.net.fw`) and chained `._` at multiple levels (`den.aspects.infra.net._` → `fw`, `dns`). The only practical ceiling is eval cost: each level is a submodule merge over a lazy attrset, so very deep/wide trees get slow, not rejected.

**What `den.aspects.foo._` includes — direct children only:**

- `._` is a plain alias of `.provides` (`lib.mkAliasOptionModule [ "_" ] [ "provides" ]` in `aspectSubmodule`). On the evaluated aspect it is `syntheticProvides = providesChildren // { __functor = … }` — the declared `provides` children (e.g. `provides.emulation`) plus a hidden `__functor` (it does not show up in `? name` / `? includes`).
- When placed in an `includes` list, that functor resolves to a synthetic aspect `foo._` whose `includes` is **all of foo's direct freeform child aspects** (e.g. `foo.bar`), merged with the `provides` children.
- **foo's own class keys are NOT included.** The synthetic `childKeys` are filtered with `!(classReg ? k)` (registered `den.classes`), so `foo.nixos`, `foo.darwin`, `foo.homeManager` and any custom class keys are excluded — they stay reachable as `den.aspects.foo.nixos` etc. The test `test-include-children-skips-class-keys` is explicit: including `mixed._` delivers `child` but the `nixos` key "must not leak" (hostName stays at the NixOS default). Same for nested aspects (`test-include-children-nested-mixed`, `test-include-children-nested-custom-class`), and structural keys (`name`, `meta`, `includes`, `excludes`, `provides`, `policies`, `classes`, …), `__*` internals, and quirk/pipe keys are all excluded too.
- **Grandchildren are NOT directly included.** `test-include-children-no-grandchildren`: `den.aspects.top._` includes `mid` and `sibling`, but `mid.deep` (the grandchild) is *not* — "mid must be explicitly included or have its own `._` for deep to resolve." Reach grandchildren by chaining: `den.aspects.foo._.bar._` (verified by `test-include-children-nested-chained`).

So: `den.aspects.foo._` = foo's direct child aspects + foo's `provides` children, nothing else — no grandchildren, no class keys. If you want foo's own config too, include `den.aspects.foo` alongside it (or just `den.aspects.foo`, which applies its class keys; note a `provides.<same-name-as-foo>` child is the "self-provide" idiom that foo applies to itself).

In den, when should a custom class be forwarded into an existing class and when should it be evaluated on its own?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**Rule of thumb: it's about where the class's content ultimately lives and gets evaluated.**

**Forward into an existing class when** the configuration *belongs to an existing class's module system* — i.e. there is a natural destination path inside a class that is already evaluated for that entity, and you just want a cleaner way to address it. den's own docstring for the `forward` battery puts it as "separating concerns on huge module hierarchies" (`modules/aspects/batteries/forward.nix`). That covers:

- **Scope splitting over an existing class**: `user` → `users.users.<name>` on the host's OS class; `homeManager` → `home-manager.users.<name>`; `hjem`, `maid`, `wsl` → subpaths of the OS class.
- **Aliases**: `hm` → `homeManager` with `adaptArgs` injecting `osConfig` (example in `docs/src/content/docs/guides/custom-class-examples.mdx`).
- **Conditional/variant slices**: platform classes (`hmLinux`/`hmDarwin` guarded on `pkgs.stdenv.is*`), role-matched classes, and guards that test the *target* — `guard = { options, ... }: options ? wsl` for "option exists", `lib.mkIf config.…` for "config value" — so the class only materializes where the target actually has that option tree.
- **Cross-class fan-out**: `os` → both `nixos` and `darwin`, `nix` → both `nixos` and `homeManager`.

Mechanics: `den.batteries.forward { each; fromClass; intoClass; intoPath; fromAspect; }` (or lower-level: register `den.classes.<name>` and add a `den.lib.policy.route`/`deliver` policy). The forwarded content is **evaluated inside the target class's module system** — it gets the target's options, module args and specialArgs (which is why guards/adaptArgs operate on the target's args), so your class never needs its own builder.

**Evaluate on its own when** the class has *its own module system and its own output* — the content doesn't fit into any existing class's option tree, and it must be evaluated by a different builder that produces its own artifact. That's the `policy.instantiate` pattern: collect the class's bucket per entity and feed it to your builder, e.g.

- **terranix** (`docs/src/content/docs/tutorials/terranix-demo.mdx`): the `terranix` class is collected via `den.lib.policy.instantiate { name = "${host.name}-tf"; class = "terranix"; instantiate = { modules, ... }: modules; intoAttr = [ "terranixModules" host.name ]; }` and becomes its own flake outputs (packages/apps/devShells) through terranix's flake-module — there is no `nixos`/`homeManager` path to forward into.
- **Standalone systems**: the microvm and nvf-standalone templates evaluate a custom class into its own package/system; note even in `templates/microvm/modules/guests-example.nix` the `microvm` *guest* class is a forwarder (`→ nixos.microvm.vms.<name>` on the server) while the guest itself is a separate host with `intoAttr = [ ]`.
- If the standalone class also needs its **own scope** (guests, fleet members, organizations), pair it with a custom entity kind: `den.schema.<kind>.inherits = [ den.schema.conf ]` + a registry via `den.lib.schema.mkInstanceType` + a `policy.resolve.to` policy (`docs/src/content/docs/guides/custom-entity-kinds.mdx`).

**Decision procedure:** (1) Is there an existing class already evaluated for this entity whose option tree has a home for your content (a subpath, an alias, a guarded slice, a fan-out)? → forward, and use `guard` when the destination only exists on some entities. (2) Is your content for a module system no existing class covers, producing its own artifact? → collect it (`policy.instantiate` / route to a flake output) and evaluate it with your own builder; add a custom entity kind if it needs its own scope.

questions.question: What is the difference between den's `policy.route` and `den.batteries.forward`, and which should I choose?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"They sit at different layers of den and do related-but-different jobs. Both verified from den's source (`denful/den`, `main`):

**`den.batteries.forward` — a battery that *creates* a custom class** (`modules/aspects/batteries/forward.nix`, machinery in `nix/lib/forward.nix`)
- It's a ready-made **aspect** you include (`den.aspects.X.includes = [ (den.batteries.forward { ... }) ]`, or via a schema include).
- Its job is to **define a new class name** and forward everything written under it into a submodule path of an existing class. Per item in `each` it takes `fromClass` (the new class to read), `intoClass` (target class), `intoPath` (attrpath), `fromAspect`, plus optional `guard` / `adaptArgs` / `adapterModule`.
- Source description: "An aspect that imports all modules defined for `from` class into a target `into` submodule … used to create custom Nix classes … returns an aspect that needs to be included for the new class to exist." This is how den implements the `homeManager`, `hjem` and `maid` classes.
- Example (docs, Custom Nix Classes): a `user` class that forwards into `users.users.<userName>` on the host's OS class, so `den.aspects.alice.user.isNormalUser = true` lands in the right place.

**`den.lib.policy.route` — a policy that *delivers* content of an existing class** (`nix/lib/policy-effects.nix`)
- It's a **policy constructor** (registered as a `den.policies.*` attribute via `den.schema.<class>.includes` — note the spelling: `den.lib.policy.route`, not `den.policy.route`).
- It **moves** content already collected under `fromClass` into `intoClass` at `path`/`intoPath`, with `reinstantiate` (verbatim) and `guard`/`adaptArgs`. The source comment is explicit: "Route class or quirk content from one scope partition into a target class. Tier 1 delivery — **replaces `den.batteries.forward` for the common case**." It's a permanent shim over `deliver` (the lower-level edge primitive): `fromClass→from`, `intoClass→to`, `path/intoPath→at`, `reinstantiate→mode="verbatim"`.
- Example (docs, Custom Nix Classes): `den.classes.files = { }; den.policies.files-to-flake-parts = _: [ (den.lib.policy.route { fromClass = "files"; intoClass = "flake-parts"; path = [ "files" ]; }) ];` — note `path`, not `intoPath`.

**Which to choose**
- **You want a *new class name* for your aspects** (so people can write `den.aspects.alice.container = { ... }`) → `den.batteries.forward` (or the built-in `den.batteries.user` for `users.users.<name>`-style forwarding). It's the ergonomic factory; den's own docs call it "the ergonomic way to build a custom class".
- **The class already exists** (registered via `den.classes.<name> = { }`) and you just need to declare where its content lands — a one-off delivery, including from a custom class → use `den.lib.policy.route` directly; the source says it's what replaces forward for the common case.
- The two compose: a `forward`-created class can later be moved with a `route` policy (den's `forward-from-custom-class.nix` example does exactly that).

Rule of thumb: **forward = "create me a class"; route = "deliver this class's content"**.

questions.question: Is `policy.when (host: host.hasAspect den.aspects.other) { nixos = ...; }` a correct use of `den.lib.policy.when` inside an aspect's includes?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Yes — that is a correct use of `den.lib.policy.when` inside an aspect's `includes`. In fact it's the exact case this combinator was built for.

**Why it works (verified against `denful/den` @ `main`):**

1. **`when` accepts an inline aspect as its second argument.** `when = predicate: policiesOrSingle` (`nix/lib/policy-effects.nix`). For a plain attrset like `{ nixos = ...; }` (not a `__isPolicy` record, not a function), `wrapAsConditional` produces a *conditional aspect*:
   `{ name = "<when>"; meta.guard = predicate; meta.aspects = [ p ]; includes = [ ]; }`
   That's an aspect-shaped record, so it belongs in `includes` just like any other aspect.

2. **`hasAspect` in a guard is the supported, cycle-free path.** The `hasAspect` entity option (`modules/context/has-aspect.nix`) is computed from `config.resolved`, and its own docs warn it is "NOT safe to use for deciding an aspect's `includes` list — that's cyclic". `when` is the exception: the compile-conditional handler (`nix/lib/aspects/fx/handlers/compile-conditional.nix`) evaluates `meta.guard` against a guard context built by `mkGuardCtx`, whose comment says it exists "so predicates written as `({ host, ... }: host.hasAspect ref)` work without touching config.resolved". It provides entity-shaped stubs — `host = { hasAspect = <pipeline hasAspect> }` — where `hasAspect` (`mkPipelineHasAspect`) is computed from the **in-flight pathSet**, scoped to the entity's own subtree plus inherited scopes (the #613 fix), and exclude-aware.

3. **The reference side works.** A bare parametric function under `den.aspects` (e.g. `den.aspects.other = { host, ... }: { ... }`) is normalized by `providerType` into a record carrying `name = "other"` and `meta.aspect-chain` (the single-def branch of `mergeFunctions`, `nix/lib/aspects/types.nix`), so `hasAspect` can key it via `identity.key`. Resolved nodes are indexed in the pathSet under the same key (both ctx-qualified and base keys — `collectPathsHandler` in `nix/lib/aspects/fx/identity.nix`), so `host.hasAspect den.aspects.other` matches when `other` is included anywhere in that entity's subtree.

4. **Ordering doesn't matter.** If the guard fails at first (e.g. `other` is included later in the walk), the conditional is deferred and re-evaluated at the entity boundary by the fixed-point `drain-conditionals` handler, so the payload fires as soon as membership becomes true.

The reference doc shows the same shape: `den.lib.policy.when ({ host, ... }: host.wsl.enable) den.policies.wsl-setup` (`docs/src/content/docs/reference/policies.mdx`). Your `(host: ...)` form is the same destructuring in lambda sugar.

**Two caveats:**

- The `host` stub only exists in scopes whose `__scopeHandlers` include `host`. If the same aspect can also be resolved in a scope *without* a host binding (e.g. a home-only scope), the conditional path calls the guard directly without the arg pre-check the policy path has, so `(host: ...)` would throw "attribute `host` missing". If that applies to your tree, write it defensively: `ctx: (ctx ? host) && ctx.host.hasAspect den.aspects.other`.
- `den.aspects.other` must be a real aspect defined under `den.aspects` — the ref is keyed by its name + aspect-chain, so a misspelling won't match anything (and a bare string won't key at all).

Also note the guard sees *scoped* membership (the entity's own + inherited subtree), not fleet-wide presence of `other`.

questions.question: Can I use den without flake-parts, or even without flakes?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Yes to both: den works without flake-parts, and without flakes.

**How it works:** den's core is a plain Nix library, not a flake dependency. In `nix/default.nix` the core is `den-lib = import ./lib` — a function you call as `den-lib { inherit inputs config lib; }`, which hands you back `nixModule` and friends. The flake-parts integration only exists as an optional convenience layer: `flakeModule` / `flakeModules` ("flake-parts conventions"). The README states it plainly: "Den embraces your Nix. With or without flakes, flake-parts, or home-manager. Zero dependencies. Every part is optional and replaceable."

**Templates that prove it** (all in `templates/`, also exposed by the flake as `templates.*`):
- `minimal` — "flakes, nothing else" (no flake-parts)
- `noflake` — "Den without flake": stable Nix only, **no flakes, no flake-parts**, and nix-maid (import-tree) instead of home-manager. Its `default.nix` is pure plain Nix: `npins` for locking + `with-inputs` for flake-like input resolution, and `lib.evalModules` with the den module. Try it with `npins update den`, then e.g. `nix-build -A flake.nixosConfigurations.igloo.config.system.build.toplevel`.

**One caveat, from `templates/noflake/README.md`:** "Den needs a top-level attribute where to place configurations. questions.question: My formatter's dead-code linter removed an unused `user` argument from a den class module, and now the module stopped applying. Why does an unused argument matter?

{ host, user }: {
  homeManager = { config, ... }: { ... };   # `user` unused in the body
}
```

questions.question: What does `builtins.functionArgs` return for `{ a, b ? 1, ... }: a`, and for a positional function `x: x`?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"`builtins.functionArgs` returns a set with **one attribute per named formal argument** of the function. Each value is a **Boolean telling you whether that argument has a default** — not the default value itself, and not `null`.

- **`{ a, b ? 1, ... }: a`** → **`{ a = false; b = true; }`**
  - `a` has no default → `false`; `b ? 1` has a default → `true`.
  - The `...` ellipsis does not produce an entry, so you cannot detect it from `functionArgs` — the result looks the same for `{ a, b ? 1 }: a` and `{ a, b ? 1, ... }: a`.

- **`x: x`** → **`{ }`** (the empty set)
  - Plain (positional) lambdas have no formal arguments, so `functionArgs` returns nothing for them.

How I know: I read the implementation `prim_functionArgs` in `src/libexpr/primops.cc` of NixOS/nix (`master`, fetched via raw.githubusercontent.com). For a lambda with formals it does `attrs.insert(i.name, state.getBool(i.def), i.pos)` — i.e. each formal maps to `true` iff it has a default expression — and when `getFormals()` is null (positional lambda) it returns `Bindings::emptyBindings`. The doc comment on `__functionArgs` in the same file, and the `functionArgs f` entry of the Nix 2.34.9 reference manual, state the same with the worked example `functionArgs ({ x, y ? 123 }: ...) = { x = false; y = true; }`.

Edge cases from the same source: if the argument is not a lambda you get a type error (`'functionArgs' requires a function`), and a partially-applied builtin also yields `{ }`.

  # -> { a = { b = 1; c = 2; } }

  Right side wins on any conflicting path; if one side's value isn't an attrset, that side's value simply replaces the other.

questions.question: Why does `1 / 2` evaluate to 0 in Nix?

function.name: reply

draft.answer:
In Nix, number types are preserved through arithmetic: both `1` and `2` are integers, so `/` between them is integer division, truncated toward zero — hence `1 / 2` = `0`. The moment one operand is a float, the result becomes a float: `1 / 2.0` (or `1.0 / 2`) evaluates to `0.5`.

How I know: the Nix reference manual (Operators → Arithmetic, v2.35.2) states that "Pure integer operations will always return integers, whereas any operation involving at least one floating point number returns a floating point number." I checked that page directly. The same section notes that division by zero and integer overflow (results outside the representable integer range) are evaluation errors.

So if you expected `0.5` in a config, make one operand a float — e.g. `ratio = 1 / 2.0` — or scale your numbers so integer division does what you want.

questions.question: My function `{ a ? 1 }: a` errors when called with `{ b = 2; }`. Why, and how do I let it accept extra attributes?

When you call it with `{ b = 2; }`, `a` falls back to its default `1` (that part is fine), but `b` is not named in the pattern and there is no `...` to swallow it, so the evaluator throws a type error at the call site. ```
error: anonymous lambda called with unexpected argument 'b'
```

**How to accept extra attributes:** add `...` to the pattern:

```nix

```

```nix

{ a ? 1, b ? null, ... }: { a = a; b = b; }

# bind the whole argument set under a name, in addition to the pattern
{ a ? 1, ... } @ args: { a = a; rest = args; }
```

    builtins.isFunction x

{"answer":"**Short answer: not on every upgrade.** Bump it only when you cross a *major* release, and follow the release notes for that release.

**What it does.** `system.stateVersion` records the last NixOS release this machine was *upgraded from*. NixOS uses it with `lib.versionOlder` / `lib.versionAtLeast` to decide which migration/upgrade logic to run when you `nixos-rebuild switch` to a new system (renaming options, moving systemd units, adjusting service config, etc.). I confirmed it's a live, current option: it shows up as `config.system.stateVersion` in current defaults — e.g. `boot.zfs.forceImportRoot` defaults to `lib.versionOlder config.system.stateVersion "26.11"`, and `boot.swraid.enable` to `"true if stateVersion is older than 23.11"`.

1. **Upgrading from release A to a new major release B** (e.g. `24.11` → `25.05`): set `system.stateVersion = "24.11"` — the release you're *coming from* — in your config, then rebuild, so the A→B migration runs.
2. **Once that generation works fine**, bump `system.stateVersion` to `"25.05"` in a follow-up commit. That stops the A→B migration from re-running on every subsequent rebuild.

questions.question: I set `users.users.me.shell = pkgs.zsh;` and the build fails with an assertion. What else do I need?

{"answer":"You're hitting NixOS's "shell program check". In current nixpkgs the users module (`nixos/modules/config/users-groups.nix`) asserts, for every user and each of the shells `fish`, `xonsh`, `zsh`:

```nix
assertion = !user.ignoreShellProgramCheck
            -> (user.shell == pkgs.zsh)
            -> (config.programs.zsh.enable == true);
```

with the message: *"users.users.me.shell is set to zsh, but programs.zsh.enable is not true. This will cause the zsh shell to lack the basic nix directories in its PATH and might make logging in as that user impossible."*

**What you need:**

```nix
programs.zsh.enable = true;
```

That option (defined in `nixos/modules/programs/zsh/zsh.nix`, default `false`) makes NixOS generate `/etc/zshenv`, which sources `system.build.setEnvironment` — that's what puts the Nix profiles on the login shell's PATH. It also adds zsh to `environment.systemPackages` and registers the shell in `environment.shells`. The option's own description says: "To enable zsh for a particular user, use the `users.users.<name>.shell` option for that user" — which is the half you already did; enabling the program module is the other half.

t.int.verify "x"  # => "expected type 'int' but value \"x\" is of type 'string'"

function.name: reply

{"answer":"**No — gen-graph's `topoOrder` does not throw on a cyclic graph.** It returns a value:

```nix
{ ok = true;  order = [ node ]; }
| { ok = false; cycles = [ [ node ]; ... ]; }
```

**What to read from the result:**

- Check `.ok`.
- **`ok = true`** → `.order` is a producers-first list of node ids: `edges u ∋ v` means "u depends on v" (consumer → producer), so every node is emitted after everything it depends on. - **`ok = false`** → no `.order` field. `.cycles` is a list of lists: the SCC member sets that lie on cycles, **all of them at once** (you don't fix one and meet the next), each group sorted within its component. A self-loop is reported as its own singleton `[ "a" ]`. Each group is a *member set of a strongly connected component*, not an ordered path — if you want an ordered loop for a human-readable message, use `cyclePaths g`, which gives one representative simple cycle per cyclic component.

questions.question: Why does gen-prelude ship its own `hasInfix` instead of using nixpkgs' `lib.hasInfix`?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Two reasons, both stated in gen-prelude's own source.

**1. Structural: gen-prelude is deliberately nixpkgs-lib-free, so `lib.hasInfix` isn't even in scope.** gen-prelude's flake declares zero inputs — the README says "The lib flake carries zero inputs, so a consumer's lock gains no transitive nixpkgs dependency from pulling gen-prelude in. Purity is enforced structurally (the flake has no inputs to draw a lib from)." Every other pure gen lib (gen-graph, gen-vars, gen-scope, gen-dispatch, gen-memo, …) depends on it as its base, so importing nixpkgs for one helper would drag nixpkgs into the whole pure substrate's closure. The README's mental model is: "wherever a pure gen lib would have written `lib.X`, it writes `prelude.X` instead and gets identical semantics with no nixpkgs.lib in its closure." That covers `hasInfix` like every other vendored utility.

**2. Behavioral: gen-prelude's copy is *not* a verbatim copy — it is a drop-in that is linear where nixpkgs' is not.** I checked both definitions:

- nixpkgs `lib/strings.nix` (master): `hasInfix = infix: … content: builtins.match ".*${escapeRegex infix}.*" "${content}" != null;`
- gen-prelude `lib/default.nix` (main): `hasInfix = infix: content: infix == "" || length (split (escapeRegex infix) content) > 1;`

The source comment explains why: the leading/trailing `.*` in nixpkgs' pattern makes std::regex recurse to depth proportional to the haystack length, which overflows the C stack (an uncatchable abort, `tryEval` doesn't contain it) when scanning whole source files — and gen-prelude's own purity scanner does exactly that: it `readFile`s the library's source and token-scans it with this `hasInfix` (the README: "The scanner is this library's own `hasInfix` scanning this library"). Splitting on the escaped literal has no `.*` anchor, so it scans linearly.

It stays a faithful drop-in: the `escapeRegex` vendored alongside it uses the same twelve metacharacters in the same order as nixpkgs' (`\[{()^$?*+|.`) with the same `replaceStrings` fold, so the escaped output is byte-identical to `lib.escapeRegex`, and the prelude-fidelity suite asserts `prelude.hasInfix input == lib.hasInfix input` over normal and boundary inputs (the README notes per-member escape arms plus byte-identity over all 95 printable ASCII). questions.question: In gen-schema I changed a `listOf str` field on an instance and its `id_hash` did not change. Is that a bug?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Not a bug — it's by design.

**What `id_hash` hashes.** The digest covers only the kind's *primitive* options. In `sini/gen-schema` (`lib/id-hash.nix`, on `main`):

```nix
primitiveTypeNames = [ "string" "str" "int" "bool" "float" ];
isPrimitiveOption =
  _name: opt:
  (opt ? type) && prelude.elem (opt.type.name or "") primitiveTypeNames && (opt.identity or true);
```

and the key set is derived as

```nix
[ "name" ]
++ prelude.attrNames (prelude.filterAttrs isPrimitiveOption (…evalModuleTree… [ kindValue ]).options)
```

i.e. `name` + every `str`/`int`/`bool`/`float`-typed option, minus `identity = false` opt-outs. The file's comment states the rule outright: *"a non-primitive option is never a key, and `identity` on one is inert"*; the README's Identity Hashing section says the same ("The pairs are all primitive options (str, int, bool, float) minus the declared opt-outs … a non-primitive option is never a key").

A `listOf str` field is non-primitive, so it never enters the digest — changing it leaves `id_hash` untouched. Same for any `attrsOf`, `ref`, `setOf`, method return, etc.

**You can verify on your own kind.** Every instance carries the closed key set as a read-only field:

```nix
config.hosts.igloo._identityKeys  # → e.g. [ "name" "addr" "role" ] — no list field
```

**If you want the list to affect identity.** There is no opt-*in* channel: naming a non-primitive in `_identity.keys` is refused by name (`_identity.keys: 'tags' is not an identity key of kind 'host' (identity keys: …)`), and the set is closed at the kind boundary, so `extraModules` on the registry can't add keys either. The working shape is to project the list into a primitive option declared on the kind itself, e.g. a `str` option whose value is a canonical encoding of the list (concatenated/sorted elements, a digest you compute yourself). That primitive then reflects like any other.

Caveats: I verified against `sini/gen-schema` `main` (read `flake.nix`, README, `lib/id-hash.nix`, `lib/instance.nix` via raw fetch — `clone` was unavailable in this environment and the GitHub API refused me), not against the exact rev you have pinned; and I did not evaluate your own flake, since I don't have its repo/rev. questions.question: In gen-schema, what happens when an instance sets a key its kind does not declare?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**It's an error — by default, a catchable eval-time `throw` that names every offending key with a fix suggestion.** Kinds are strict by default (`strict = true` in `mkSchemaOption`; `mkInstanceType`/`mkInstanceRegistry` inherit it via `strict ? kindValue.strict`), and strictness is implemented by `mkStrictModule` being imported into every instance.

**Mechanism** (`lib/strict.nix`): the module injects `config._module.freeformType` (via `merge.mkDefault`) set to a type whose `merge` *always throws*. The module system's freeform capture collects any def value the option tree didn't consume; the throw then walks those values against the kind's `options` tree (`unmatchedPaths`) to name the key — the first name the tree does not declare, at its path under the instance (a key inside a nested submodule is captured at that submodule's level, not the kind's). The message is a `throw`, so `builtins.tryEval` catches it. Exact shape (README "Strict Validation" + the `throw` in `strict.nix`):

```
STRICT MODE: "addrr", "net.mtuu" are not declared on host (instance at hosts.web, defined in /etc/nixos/hosts.nix).
Fix: schema.host.options.addrr = mkOption { ... };
Fix: schema.host.options.net.mtuu = mkOption { ... };
```

Keys are rendered as parseable Nix source (quoted/escaped per nixpkgs' identifier rules), so the printed `Fix:` line declares exactly the key it names.

**Opt-outs**, in order of scope:
- Per registry: `mkInstanceRegistry { strict = false; }`
- Per kind: `config.schema.host._module.freeformType = lib.types.attrsOf lib.types.anything;`
- Globally: `mkSchemaOption { strict = false; }`

In the non-strict branch, `mkInstanceType` sets `config._module.freeformType = merge.types.attrsOf merge.types.anything` (`lib/instance.nix`), so undeclared keys are simply admitted and carried into the instance.

questions.question: How do I run a gen library's tests locally, and why is `nix flake check` at the repo root not enough?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"## Running a gen library's tests locally

From the repo root of any gen library:

```bash
nix develop ./ci --command ci                 # the suite (guarded), then every declared check except tests-error
nix develop ./ci --command ci --tests-error   # the error plane (guarded), then checks.tests-error
```

- `ci` is the **guarded** form of `nix-unit --flake ./ci#tests`, and then builds every declared check (one `nix build` per check, so each failing one is named). The two commands together are what the harness calls the local gate: every declared check, guarded.
- The error plane is separate by construction: cells whose `expr` can *abort* cannot live in `flake.tests`, because the batch asserter behind `checks.default` forces every `expr` unconditionally (an aborting one crashes the gate). They sit on `flake.testsError` (e.g. `ci/tests-error.nix`) and run via `--tests-error`.
- A single suite: `nix-unit --flake ./ci#tests.<suite>.<name>` works, but is the unguarded form. The harness also wires the same guard into `ci` / `ci-error` pre-commit hooks.

## Why `nix flake check` at the repo root is not enough

Two independent reasons:

1. **The root flake contains no tests.** A library's root flake exports only its `lib`. I read `sini/gen-graph`'s `main` `flake.nix`: its entire output set is `lib = import ./. { prelude = gen-prelude.lib; };` — there is no `checks` attribute at all. So `nix flake check` at the root only confirms the root flake *evaluates*; it runs zero test cells. The suite is a **separate flake**, `ci/flake.nix` (own `flake.lock`, own inputs: `gen-harness` + `nixpkgs`), built on `gen-harness.lib.mkCi` with `testModules = ./tests`, which import-trees the whole `ci/tests/` directory — a new test file becomes a gate the moment it lands.

2. **Even `nix flake check ./ci` is the unguarded variant.** The suite's evaluator reads a *git-filtered* copy of the repo, so any file git doesn't know about — untracked, gitignored — is simply absent from the source the cells are collected from. Add `ci/tests/new-guard.nix`, forget to `git add` it, and the run is byte-identical to the run without it: green over the cell it cannot see. The guarded entry points (the `ci` devshell command, and the `ci`/`ci-error` pre-commit hooks) refuse *before* nix-unit is reached if anything under the declared read roots is git-unknown; the remedy is `git add` (or move the file out from under the root). The guard does not refuse tracked-modified, tracked-deleted or staged files — those are fully visible to the evaluator with their worktree bytes.

## How I know

- `sini/gen` (hub) README, "What it promises" / "How it's architected": all 23 library repos build their `ci/flake.nix` on `gen-harness.lib.mkCi`; `nix develop ./ci --command ci` is the guarded run; bare `nix flake check ./ci` is unguarded.
- `sini/gen-graph` `main`: `flake.nix` (single `lib` output, no `checks`) and `ci/flake.nix` (`mkCi` with `testModules = ./tests`, `tests-error.nix` on `extraModules`).
- `sini/gen-harness` `main` README: the "declared read domain" section (git-filtered source, the byte-identical untracked-file failure mode) and its command list, which states `nix develop ./ci --command ci` is "the command to run the suites and checks by".

questions.question: In the gen ecosystem, can a substrate library like gen-graph depend on gen-aspects?

function.name: reply

{"answer":"**No — by the ecosystem's layering the edge points the other way.** gen-graph is a substrate and gen-aspects is the domain layer above it; a substrate that depended on gen-aspects would invert the dependency, which is exactly the failure mode gen-graph's README names.

What the sources show (all on `main` of `sini/*`):

1. **gen-graph's flake has exactly one input: gen-prelude.** `sini/gen-graph` `flake.nix`: `inputs = { gen-prelude.url = "github:sini/gen-prelude"; }`, with the comment "gen-graph is nixpkgs-lib-free: the library depends only on gen-prelude (pure, zero-input). It is pure graph/list/attr combinators — no module system, no nixpkgs.lib."

2. **gen-aspects doesn't even take gen-graph as a flake input.** Its flake inputs are gen-prelude, gen-merge, gen-schema, gen-identity, gen-algebra. The edge between the two is drawn at the consumer: gen-aspects *states* the graph as plain data (`graphFacts`: "the node set, the edge relations and the node values — as plain data … every fact here is an attrset, a list or a string"), and the framework "builds the graph from these with `gen-graph.fromRegistry`". gen-aspects' README states the direction outright: "gen-aspects imports no query library for this: the query libraries are needed to *query* a graph, never to *state* one."

And on `seededFixpoint`: gen-scope ships a well-founded model, "but it is unreachable from gen-graph by layering rather than by absence: gen-scope takes gen-graph as a flake input, so consuming it here would invert the dependency."

questions.question: Which gen library mints identities, and what does an identity look like?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**gen-identity** (`sini/gen-identity`) is the one. The gen hub describes it as "the ecosystem's single minting authority: hashIdentity … so structurally equal values mint one identity", and the library's own source states it more pointedly: "`hashIdentity` is the one minting authority; nothing else mints (ADR-0016 ruling 5)". It is dependency-free (builtins only) precisely so any other library can take it without a cycle.

**What an identity looks like:** a single string of the form

```
"<kind>:" + <64-char sha256 hex digest>
```

e.g. `"bobbin:9e7fccd3…"`. The kind tag rides *outside* the digest, so the kind is recoverable by splitting on the first colon and a trace reads directly. The digest is `builtins.hashString "sha256"` over a **bounded, type-tagged canonical encoding** of the `⟨label, value⟩` pairs — the preimage, not the raw value.

From the source (`sini/gen-identity`, `lib/default.nix`, `main`):

```nix
hashIdentity =
  kind: labels: valueOf:
  …
  else
    "${builtins.unsafeDiscardStringContext kind}:"
    + builtins.hashString "sha256" (canonicalPreimage kind labels valueOf);
```

Practical shape of the call: `hashIdentity : kind -> [labels] -> (label -> value) -> "<kind>:<sha256hex>"`, e.g. `hashIdentity "bobbin" [ "name" "thread" ] (k: { name = "lark"; thread = "linen"; }.${k})`.

Rules that follow from the same file:

- **Admitted values:** strings, bools, ints, floats with `|v| < 2^53` (integral floats normalise to their int rendering), `null`, and lists/attrsets of those to bounded depth (512) and preimage length (65536). Every node carries a type tag (`s`/`b`/`i`/`f`/`z`/`[…]`/`{…}`) so a string can never forge as a list; `toJSON` is applied to strings only — structure is emitted, never delegated.
- **Refused by name (no identity at all):** lambdas (no builtin exposes a closure's body), paths (`toJSON` copies them to the store), derivations (self-referential `out` attribute), floats outside the exact-int range, a non-string/empty kind, a kind containing `:`, zero labels, a non-string label, a duplicate label. A refusal names the kind (and the label inside a walk) and never the value.
- **Order-insensitivity is by construction:** labels are rendered as an attrset and emitted via sorted `attrNames`, so `[ "user" "host" ]` and `[ "host" "user" ]` mint the same identity.

One related boundary: the *reflection* half stays in **gen-schema** (deciding which of a kind's options are identity keys, recomputing an instance's `id_hash`, stamping it via `mkIdentityModule`) — that library calls into the gen-identity mint rather than minting itself.

questions.question: Can a gen library use `nixpkgs.lib` functions?

{"answer":"**No — not in the library's own source. That's an enforced invariant, not a style preference.**

Every roster library's `lib/` must be **nixpkgs-lib-free**. Each repo carries a source scanner (`ci/tests/purity.nix`; `gen-types` has it as `ci/tests/types-purity.nix`) that scans the library source for the tokens `lib.`, `{ lib }` / `{ lib,`, `evalModules`, `mkOption` and `nixpkgs`, and a hit fails CI (`nix develop ./ci --command ci purity`). - **`gen-prelude`** — a zero-dependency utility base: builtins re-exports plus pure list/attrset/string helpers *vendored behaviour-identically from `nixpkgs.lib`*, "so every other library can drop nixpkgs from its closure." - **Full nixpkgs only at the terminals** — `nixpkgs.lib.nixosSystem` and friends enter via the terminals a realization is handed (the hub's interim `flakeModules.default` supplies the sanctioned default; a consumer may override it). The invariant across the crossing is values-injection, never type-driving: gen types never enter the consumer's options tree, so nixpkgs never type-walks them.

Yes — den is explicitly built for this, and den's own repo ships a working example of exactly your shape (no hosts, custom class only): the `nvf-standalone` template. There are two ways to do it.

**1. As a pure library: `den.lib.aspects.resolve <class> <aspect>`**

`den.lib.aspects.resolve` (documented in `docs/src/content/docs/reference/lib.mdx`) resolves an aspect for one class and returns a module: in `nix/lib/aspects/fx/resolve.nix` it is defined as

```nix
fxResolve = mkPipeline: args: { inherit (fxResolveFull mkPipeline args) imports; };
```

i.e. it returns `{ imports = [ ... ]; }` — the collected class modules from the whole aspect tree (`includes`, `provides`, forward batteries), with den context args already partially applied where a context exists. You then evaluate the list yourself with your own module system. This is exactly what den's own template does in `templates/nvf-standalone/modules/nvf-integration.nix`:

```nix
module = den.lib.aspects.resolve "nvf" aspect;   # { imports = [...]; }
...
(inputs.nvf.lib.neovimConfiguration { modules = [ module ]; }).neovim;  # user's own eval
```

So your version would look like:

```nix
myEval = pkgs:
  let
    collected = den.lib.aspects.resolve "myclass" den.aspects.root;
  in
  (lib.evalModules {
    modules = [ your-options collected ];  # collected is { imports = [...]; }
    specialArgs = { inherit pkgs; };
  }).config;
```

There's also `den.lib.aspects.resolveImports` (same, but skips entity instantiation — for nested extraction), and `den.lib.resolveEntity <kind> <ctx>` if you want the aspect driven by an entity record: the docs' own example is `den.lib.aspects.resolve "flake" (den.lib.resolveEntity "flake" { })`.

```nix

den.schema.flake-system.includes = [ den.aspects.flake ];
den.aspects.flake.packages = { pkgs, ... }: { my-neovim = ...; };
```

and its flake.nix is just `nixpkgs.lib.evalModules { modules = [ ... ]; }.config.flake` — den's flake policies (`modules/policies/flake.nix`) register `packages`/`apps`/`checks`/`devShells`/`legacyPackages` as classes and route them into `config.flake.<output>.<system>` with `pkgs = inputs.nixpkgs.legacyPackages.<system>` attached. questions.question: Does using den make Nix evaluation of my NixOS systems slower than wiring nixosSystem by hand?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"**Short answer: no meaningful difference — den ends up calling the same `nixosSystem` you'd wire by hand, and the overhead it adds is a small amount of pure Nix evaluation, not a new evaluation mechanism.** I checked den's source (`denful/den`, `main`) because I had no eval access in this thread to benchmark your specific setup.

**1. The system build is the same call.** In `nix/lib/entities/host.nix`, the default for a host's `instantiate` is:

```nix
default =
  {
    nixos = inputs.nixpkgs.lib.nixosSystem;
    darwin = inputs.darwin.lib.darwinSystem;
    ...
  } .${config.class};
```

So for a NixOS host, den assembles a module list from your resolved aspects (`host.mainModule`) and hands it to `inputs.nixpkgs.lib.nixosSystem` — the very function you'd call manually. The dominant cost of any NixOS evaluation (the module system walking thousands of NixOS modules) is identical, given the same set of modules. den is a zero-dependency pure-Nix library: nothing to build, no subprocesses, no codegen at eval time.

**2. What den adds on top** is pure Nix expression evaluation: resolving your aspect tree per scope, policy/scope routing, and collecting class modules into `mainModule`. That's real extra work, but it's Nix-only and small next to the module-system cost.

**3. den did have measurable eval overhead — and fixed it in current main.** PR #579 (merged May 31, 2026) is the record:
- *Closure-chain elimination*: its state helpers wrapped accumulated state in `_: ...` thunks, creating O(N) closure chains; with ~2,900 reads that was O(N²). Fix (materialise state eagerly): **cold eval −17%, memory −70%, attrset copies −88%** (den-internal before/after, not vs. a hand-wired baseline). Pre-fix, deep NixOS module trees (stylix + plasma-manager + sops-nix) could stack-overflow under den.
- *Lazy instantiation*: `applyInstantiates`/`hostConfigs` now defer `spec.instantiate` behind thunks, so a multi-host flake only evaluates the hosts you actually access. Before that fix, den could force-evaluate all hosts' NixOS configs — that was the one place den was genuinely slower than hand wiring (a hand-written attrset of `nixosSystem` calls is lazy per attribute by construction).

**4. Where den can legitimately cost more than a minimal hand-wired config:**
- Scope fan-out: den resolves the whole aspect tree per scope (host → users → homes). If an aspect/user battery contributes to the host's NixOS config, that work happens when the host is evaluated; a hand-wired `nixosSystem` wouldn't do it.
- Batteries that emit to multiple classes (e.g. `unfree`, `primary-user`) pull in more modules than the minimal config.
- If you run den on flake-parts, `perSystem` forces all systems — but that's flake-parts, not den; hand wiring on flake-parts pays the same.

**Practical advice:** stay on current den (with #579 in it — anything from before May 2026 had the eager-instantiation behavior). If you suspect slowness, measure: `time nix eval .#nixosConfigurations.<host>.config.system.build.toplevel.drvPath` on your den flake, then time the identical module list fed to `nixosSystem` by hand. questions.question: Is a den policy essentially a transition function in a pipeline over my hosts and users?

function.name: reply
function.arguments:
{"answer":"Mostly — with one important correction: in den, the **policy is not the transition function; the pipeline is**. A policy is the *state-parameterized action generator* that feeds it.

What the source says (read from `sini/den` @ `main`):

- **Type of a policy.** `nix/lib/aspects/policy-type.nix` defines it as `"policy function (context -> effects list)"`, wrapped as `{ __isPolicy, name, fn }`. The header of `nix/lib/policy-effects.nix` says it plainly: *"Policies return lists of these; the pipeline dispatches on `__policyEffect`."* So a policy is a partial function `ctx → [effect]`, not a state machine.
- **Where it fires.** `nix/lib/aspects/fx/policy/dispatch.nix` (`dispatchAspect`) runs a policy only when `resolveArgsSatisfied` — i.e. its destructured args (`{ host, ... }`, `{ user, ... }`) are present in the current context (per `nix/lib/synthesize-policies.nix`: *"Policies with { system, ... }: won't fire with empty ctx"*) — and it has not fired before in this scope (`firedPolicies` memo, one fire per policy name).
- **The transition function.** `nix/lib/aspects/fx/pipeline.nix` builds `mkPipeline` as an `fx.handle` effect-handler chain (the `nix-effects` trampoline) over a state that *is* the scope tree: `currentScope`, `scopeContexts`, `scopeParent` (a parent map), per-scope registries of routes/provides/pipes/spawns, and `firedPolicyNames`. The state-transition step is the handler chain itself: `(state, effect) → (new state, continuation)`.
- **What moves the state.** The effects, not the policies. In particular `resolve` — whose constructor comment in `policy-effects.nix` says *"Each resolve creates a parallel branch — a sibling context with new bindings merged into parent"* — is materialized by `handlers/push-scope.nix`, which *"atomically sets currentScope, scopeContexts, scopeParent"*. The other effect types (`validEffectTypes` in dispatch.nix: `include`, `exclude`, `route`, `instantiate`, `provide`, `pipe`, `spawn`) are actions/outputs, mostly delivery edges `(S, T, P, M)` between class buckets — which matches the README's one-liner: *"Policy — how entities relate: topology and routing between them."*

- The versioning page (`releases.mdx`) says: the v0.x series *"does not mean it is unstable"* — 180+ CI tests, fast-paced development shaped by its current users, and: *"If you would like something to be possible with Den, now is the time when all users help shape Den."*
